name: Primary headache associated with sexual activity

clinicalPearls: Headache precipitated by sexual activity, occurring either as a dull bilateral ache that builds with arousal or as an explosive headache at orgasm
The explosive orgasmic form can be indistinguishable from the thunderclap headache of subarachnoid haemorrhage on first presentation
A first or severe episode therefore mandates exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage and other vascular causes
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is an important cause of recurrent orgasmic thunderclap headache
It is more common in men and in people who also have migraine
The primary form is often self-limiting but may recur in bouts and can respond to preventive treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Primary headache associated with sexual activity is linked to the abrupt rises in blood pressure, heart rate and muscular and intracranial pressure that accompany sexual excitement and orgasm, in the absence of a structural lesion. The explosive subtype coincides with the autonomic surge at orgasm. Because the same haemodynamic stress can precipitate aneurysmal rupture or reversible vasoconstriction, secondary causes must be excluded before the primary diagnosis is accepted.
additionalInvestigations: Urgent CT of the head and, if non-diagnostic, lumbar puncture for the first severe episode
CT or MR angiography and venography for vascular causes
MRI of the brain where indicated
Repeat vascular imaging if reversible cerebral vasoconstriction is suspected
redFlags: First explosive orgasmic headache (treat as possible subarachnoid haemorrhage)
Focal neurological deficit, seizures or reduced consciousness
Recurrent thunderclap episodes suggesting vasoconstriction syndrome
reference.prognosis: Once secondary causes are excluded the primary form is benign and frequently remits over weeks to months, though it may recur; preventive treatment can help during symptomatic bouts.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign cause for a first explosive orgasmic headache without imaging
Failing to consider reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome in recurrent cases
Overlooking arterial dissection when there is neck pain
Not re-evaluating if the headache pattern changes
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Preventive treatment during symptomatic bouts with a beta-blocker such as propranolol to suppress the exertional headache
On-demand prophylaxis with indometacin or a triptan taken shortly before sexual activity to abort the orgasmic headache
Behavioural advice to reduce exertion, adopt a more passive role and temporarily abstain during a symptomatic cluster
Optimise cardiovascular risk factors and control any coexisting hypertension that amplifies the orgasmic pressure surge
Mandatory exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage and other vascular causes on the first or a severe episode before the primary label is accepted
Actively investigate for reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome in recurrent orgasmic thunderclap attacks, with a calcium channel blocker such as nimodipine if confirmed
Reassure regarding the benign, frequently self-remitting course, with neurology referral if attacks are refractory or the picture is atypical
